Hurt at Work in Washington: Why You Usually Cannot Sue Your Employer, and the Third Party Claim You Can Bring

Justin D. Leigh, Attorney-at-Law·8 min read·November 11, 2026

You were on a ladder on a commercial job in Spokane Valley when a delivery truck backed into it, and you came down on the concrete with your wrist under you. Your foreman filled out a report, a claim number from L&I came in the mail, and time-loss checks started a few weeks later. Someone on the crew told you that is all there is, because in Washington you cannot sue your employer. That is mostly true. What nobody mentioned is that the driver of that truck does not work for your employer, and Washington law treats him very differently.

Can I sue my employer for a work injury in Washington?

Almost never, and the statute says so in strong terms. RCW 51.04.010 declares that "sure and certain relief for workers, injured in their work, and their families and dependents is hereby provided regardless of questions of fault and to the exclusion of every other remedy, proceeding or compensation, except as otherwise provided in this title." It then abolishes "all civil actions and civil causes of action for such personal injuries," again except as the title provides.

RCW 51.32.010(1) repeats the trade from the worker's side. Each worker injured in the course of employment receives compensation under the chapter, and that payment is "in lieu of any and all rights of action whatsoever against any person whomsoever," except as the title otherwise provides.

That is the bargain. You do not have to prove your employer was careless to get benefits, and your own carelessness does not take them away. In exchange, a negligence lawsuit against your employer is off the table. But both sections say "except as otherwise provided in this title," and chapter 51.24 RCW provides two ways back into court.

The narrow exception: an employer who meant to cause the injury

RCW 51.24.020 is the first. If injury results to a worker "from the deliberate intention of his or her employer to produce such injury," the worker may take benefits under the title and also has a cause of action against the employer "as if this title had not been enacted, for any damages in excess of compensation and benefits paid or payable."

Read the words carefully. The statute is about an intention to produce the injury, not about how unsafe the job was. A missing guard, a skipped safety rule, or a supervisor who should have known better, without more, describes negligence, and negligence is exactly what RCW 51.04.010 takes out of the courts. Whether a particular set of facts reaches deliberate intention is a question to put to a lawyer with the whole record in hand, not one to assume either way.

The third party claim: the lawsuit many injured workers do not know they have

RCW 51.24.030(1) is the second way back into court, and it is the one that comes up far more often: "If a third person, not in a worker's same employ, is or may become liable to pay damages on account of a worker's injury for which benefits and compensation are provided under this title, the injured worker or beneficiary may elect to seek damages from the third person."

A third person is someone other than your employer who is not a co-worker. The driver of the truck that hit the ladder. The manufacturer of a saw with a guard that failed, which is a product liability claim under chapter 7.72 RCW. Another contractor on a multi-employer site. The driver who ran a red light while you were driving for work. In each, your L&I claim continues, and the third party claim runs beside it as an ordinary injury case.

There are limits worth knowing. RCW 51.24.035 bars most claims against an architect or engineer retained on a construction project, unless that professional assumed responsibility for safety by a negotiated contract or actually controlled the area where you were hurt, and the immunity does not cover negligently prepared plans. RCW 51.24.030(4) says underinsured motorist benefits are subject to the chapter only if the owner of the policy is your employer, so your own UIM coverage is treated differently from your employer's.

What the third party claim recovers

A workers' compensation claim pays the benefits Title 51 provides. A third party claim is a claim for damages, proved the way any other injury case is proved.

Because it is an ordinary injury claim, it runs on an ordinary deadline. For most claims that is three years under RCW 4.16.080(2). If the third party is a product manufacturer or seller, RCW 7.72.060(3) runs three years from when you discovered or should have discovered the harm and its cause. A claim against a city, county, or the state has to be presented before suit. The L&I claim does not stop any of those clocks.

L&I gets paid back: the lien and the distribution under RCW 51.24.060

The department, or a self-insured employer, has a direct stake in your third party case. RCW 51.24.030(2) requires the plaintiff to give the department or self-insurer notice when the action is filed, and allows it to intervene to protect its statutory interest. RCW 51.24.060(2) makes the recovery subject to a lien for the department's share.

RCW 51.24.060(1) then sets the order of distribution. Costs and reasonable attorney fees are shared proportionately between the worker and the department or self-insurer. The worker receives 25 percent of the balance, though in a settlement the worker may agree to less. The department or self-insurer is paid the balance, but only to the extent needed to reimburse benefits paid, and its reimbursement is reduced by its proportionate share of the fees and costs, a share the statute caps at 100 percent of them. Any remaining balance goes to the worker.

Then comes the part people miss. Under RCW 51.24.060(1)(e), after a recovery no further benefits are paid for the injury until the further compensation and benefits equal the remaining balance the worker received, less the department's proportionate share of fees and costs on that balance. After that, benefits resume as though there had been no recovery. Under RCW 51.24.060(3), the department or self-insurer has sole discretion to compromise its lien. RCW 51.24.060(6) provides that the distribution is confirmed by a department order under RCW 51.52.050, which means it can be protested or appealed like any other order.

If you do not bring it, the department can

The choice to pursue a third party is an election, and it has a deadline that can be forced. Under RCW 51.24.070, the department or self-insurer may serve a written demand that you elect. Unless you elect within 60 days of receiving it, and unless the action is filed or settled within the time the department allows, you are deemed to have assigned the action to the department or self-insurer.

An assignment changes who controls the case. Under RCW 51.24.050, the department or self-insurer may then prosecute or compromise the action in its discretion, and after its expenses the worker is paid 25 percent of the balance before the department is reimbursed. An election demand is not mail to set aside.

How long do I have to file an L&I claim?

One year. RCW 51.28.050 provides that no application is valid, and no claim under it enforceable, unless filed within one year after the day the injury occurred, or after the rights of dependents or beneficiaries accrued. The section points to two exceptions. RCW 51.28.055 governs occupational disease, which runs on a different clock. And under RCW 51.28.025(5), if the director determines the employer engaged in claim suppression and the worker therefore did not file, the director may in his or her sole discretion waive the time limit, provided the complaint of suppression was received within two years of the accident or exposure and the claim is filed within ninety days of the determination.

The deadline is yours, whatever the employer says about the paperwork.

My L&I claim was denied. Do I sue?

No, and this is a common misunderstanding about workers' compensation in Washington. A denial, a closure, or a disputed benefit is an order of the Department of Labor and Industries, and it is challenged inside the system, not by a lawsuit against your employer.

RCW 51.52.050(2)(a) allows anyone aggrieved by a department decision to request reconsideration from the department or to appeal to the Board of Industrial Insurance Appeals. Under RCW 51.52.050(1)(d), a final order states on its face that it becomes final within 60 days from the date it was communicated by nonelectronic means, or 65 days if communicated electronically, unless reconsideration is requested or an appeal is filed. RCW 51.52.060(1)(a) requires a notice of appeal to the Board within sixty days from the day the order was communicated, before any appeal to the courts.

Superior court comes only after the Board. RCW 51.52.110 allows an appeal to superior court within thirty days after the Board's final decision is communicated, in the county where the worker lives or where the injury occurred, and the Board's certified record becomes the record in that appeal. Even then it is an appeal of the Board's decision, not a lawsuit against your employer.

Where this goes wrong

The worker assumes the L&I claim is the whole case and never asks who else was on the site, whose truck it was, or who made the machine.

An election demand under RCW 51.24.070 sits unanswered in a stack of department mail, and the third party action is deemed assigned.

A third party case is settled without accounting for the lien and the offset under RCW 51.24.060, and the worker learns afterward that future benefits are on hold.

A denial order is treated as the last word, or as something to fight in a lawsuit, and the time to protest or appeal runs out.

The equipment that failed is repaired, scrapped, or returned to a rental company before anyone has looked at it.

The worker waits on the employer to file and the one-year limit in RCW 51.28.050 passes.

What a lawyer does here

The work is finding out whether anyone outside the employment relationship caused the injury, and doing it while the evidence still exists: the other vehicle, the equipment, the site, the contracts that say who controlled what. It is coordinating the third party case with the L&I claim, so that notice is given, election demands are answered, and the lien and offset are part of every settlement discussion rather than a surprise after it. And it is keeping every deadline straight, because a work injury can carry three or four of them on different clocks.
